source_text: En verum intellectorem operis Dei, en fidelem sapientiae eius praedicatorem. Verecundiora, inquit, nostra maiore honestate conteguntur
pass_a_gloss: Behold true intellectorem of-the-work of-God, behold fidelem sapientiae his/its praedicatorem. Verecundiora, he-says, our greater honestate conteguntur.
pass_b_english: “Much more, the members of our body that seem weak are necessary. Those members of the body which we think less honorable we surround with greater honor; and our modest parts have greater dignity, while our presentable parts need nothing. But God has arranged the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it, so that there may be no division in the body, but its members may have the same care for one another” (1 Corinthians 12:22–25).
Look at the true interpreter of God’s work! Look at the faithful herald of his wisdom! “Our modest parts,” he says, “are covered with greater dignity.”

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

bible_refs.note: Linked from Julian's wording or a clear allusion in the excerpt.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
